concepts.name: SQLite WAL checkpointing
concepts.reason: The sources define checkpointing and describe its automatic and application initiated behavior, concurrency, performance, and WAL growth.

concepts.name: Checkpoint modes
concepts.reason: SQLite provides distinct checkpoint modes with different blocking, completion, and truncation behavior.

concepts.name: Automatic checkpoint configuration
concepts.reason: SQLite documents configurable automatic checkpoint thresholds and how callbacks affect that mechanism.

concepts.name: Checkpoint progress and reader interference
concepts.reason: Readers can limit checkpoint progress and prevent WAL reset until they stop using WAL content.

concepts.name: WAL size and checkpoint performance tradeoffs
concepts.reason: Checkpoint frequency affects WAL size, read performance, write performance, syncing, and commit latency.

concepts.name: WAL writer and reader concurrency
concepts.reason: This is a related database concurrency topic rather than a child concept specific to checkpointing.

claims.text: A checkpoint transfers transactions appended in the WAL file back into the original database.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: SQLite automatically checkpoints by default when a commit causes the WAL to reach at least 1000 pages.
claims.quote: By default, SQLite does a checkpoint automatically when the WAL file reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages.

claims.text: An application can disable automatic checkpoints and run checkpoints during idle periods or in another thread or process.
claims.quote: Or they can turn off the automatic checkpoints and run checkpoints during idle moments or in a separate thread or process.

claims.text: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers but must stop before overwriting a database page past a current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: A long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.
claims.quote: Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.

claims.text: The checkpointer stores its progress in the wal-index and resumes from that point on a later invocation.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: A writer can rewind the WAL to its beginning only after all WAL content has been transferred and synced and no readers use the WAL.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: As the WAL grows, read performance deteriorates because checking the WAL takes time proportional to its size.
claims.quote: On the other hand, read performance deteriorates as the WAL file grows in size since each reader must check the WAL file for the content and the time needed to check the WAL file is proportional to the size of the WAL file.

claims.text: Checkpointing requires syncing the WAL before transferring its content to the database and syncing the database before resetting the WAL.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: Checkpoints are slower than write transactions because they require syncs and typically include many seek operations.
claims.quote: These factors combine to make checkpoints slower than write transactions.

claims.text: By default, commits grow the WAL to about 1000 pages, after which each subsequent commit runs a checkpoint until the WAL is reset below that size.
claims.quote: The default strategy is to allow successive write transactions to grow the WAL until the WAL becomes about 1000 pages in size, then to run a checkpoint operation for each subsequent COMMIT until the WAL is reset to be smaller than 1000 pages.

claims.text: By default, the commit that pushes the WAL over its size limit runs the automatic checkpoint in the same thread and can therefore be much slower.
claims.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

claims.text: More frequent checkpoints tend to favor read performance, while less frequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost across more writes.
claims.quote: To maximize the read performance, one wants to keep the WAL as small as possible and hence run checkpoints frequently, perhaps as often as every COMMIT. To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint triggers an automatic checkpoint after a commit when the WAL has at least N frames.
claims.quote: The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Passing zero or a negative N to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint disables automatic checkpoints entirely.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Registering sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint replaces an existing wal-hook callback, and registering a wal-hook callback disables this automatic checkpoint mechanism.
claims.quote: The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() . Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: Each new database connection defaults to automatic checkpointing at 1000 pages or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.
claims.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: PASSIVE checkpoints process as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers and may remain unfinished when either is concurrent.
claims.quote: Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode.

claims.text: FULL mode waits until there is no writer and all readers use the most recent database snapshot, then checkpoints all log frames and syncs the database.
claims.quote: This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot. It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.

claims.text: FULL mode blocks new writers while pending but allows new readers to continue without interruption.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: RESTART adds to FULL the wait for all readers to use only the database file, ensuring the next writer restarts the log at its beginning.
claims.quote: This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: TRUNCATE adds to RESTART truncation of the log file to zero bytes just before successful return.
claims.quote: This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: NOOP always checkpoints zero frames and can be used to read WAL and checkpoint frame counts through output parameters.
claims.quote: The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: Every sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 call obtains an exclusive checkpoint lock; if another process is checkpointing concurrently, the call returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.
claims.quote: If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: FULL, RESTART, and TRUNCATE also obtain an exclusive writer lock and invoke the busy handler while waiting for that lock or for readers.
claims.quote: The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes also obtain the exclusive "writer" lock on the database file.

claims.text: If the busy handler returns zero while FULL, RESTART, or TRUNCATE waits for a writer lock or readers, the operation continues like PASSIVE and returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

claims.text: A checkpoint can be initiated through sqlite3_wal_checkpoint, sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2, or the SQL wal_checkpoint pragma.
claims.quote: An application can initiate a checkpoint using any writable database connection on the database simply by invoking sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() or sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() .

claims.text: The automatic checkpoint threshold can be changed or automatic checkpointing disabled using wal_autocheckpoint or sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint.
claims.quote: The automatic checkpoint threshold can be changed or automatic checkpointing can be completely disabled using the wal_autocheckpoint pragma or by calling the sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() C interface.

claims.text: A checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL; SQLite usually reuses it by overwriting from the beginning.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: If overlapping readers ensure at least one reader is always active, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL can grow without bound.
claims.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Reader gaps can prevent checkpoint starvation when checkpoints are attempted during periods with no database readers.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoints ensure completion before returning but can block readers while the checkpoint runs.
claims.quote: The disadvantage of using SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE is that readers might block while the checkpoint is running.

claims.text: A checkpoint cannot complete while another transaction is running, so a large write transaction can cause the WAL to become large before the transaction ends.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.

limitations: The supplied evidence is limited to one SQLite WAL guide and two SQLite C interface reference pages; no independent sources or contrary accounts were provided.
No history or disagreement about checkpoint behavior is present in the supplied evidence.
The guide says FULL and RESTART are the modes requiring sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2, but later refers to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESET; that inconsistency cannot be resolved from the packet.
